Welding Engineer (IWE)

with practical experience as a welder, instructor, and technical consultant.

I have worked with production tasks, welder training, and welding process optimization. I specialize in MIG/MAG welding technologies, shielding gas selection, quality control, and practical implementation of solutions in production.

Author of the book “MAG/MIG Welding — from equipment selection to gas selection” (2024).

defectReduction.title: Welding defect reduction
problems: Porosity, lack of fusion, burn-through, undercut, or unstable weld shape.
Recurring rejects without a clear root cause.
Different results between shifts, welders, or batches.
Rework increases lead time and production cost.
causes: Parameters, edge preparation, gas flow, or access to the joint are not aligned.
Actual shop-floor practice differs from the process sheet or WPS.
analysisItems: Checking welding parameters, gas flow, wire stickout, and edge preparation.
Reviewing base material, filler wire, shielding gas, and weld pool protection conditions.
Matching defect patterns to the real production environment.
Checking whether the work follows the process sheet or WPS, if one exists.
solutionSteps: Define likely defect causes and verify them on samples or a production batch.
Adjust parameters, preparation, shielding, or process control points.
expectedResults: A clear defect cause or a shortlist of likely causes.
Practical corrections to parameters and process steps.
Fewer rejects and less rework.
More stable quality between shifts and operators.

processOptimization.title: Welding process stability
problems: The process is unstable and depends on a specific welder.
Parameters are adjusted manually without a clear operating window.
Productivity is low or the workflow has unnecessary steps.
Quality is acceptable, but production cost is too high.
causes: There is no fixed working window or common rules for making the weld.
Equipment, fixtures, preparation, and consumables are treated separately instead of as one system.
analysisItems: Reviewing current welding parameters, operation sequence, and access to the joint.
Checking equipment, fixtures, consumables, and workplace organization.
Comparing the actual process with product and customer requirements.
Finding bottlenecks: arc time, preparation, cleaning, rework, gas use, and wire consumption.
solutionSteps: Define the working parameter range and process constraints.
Clarify operation sequence, control points, and practical instructions for production.
expectedResults: A more stable welding parameter window.
Less dependence on individual operator habits.
Reduced downtime, rework, and unnecessary material consumption.
Clear recommendations for production and technologists.

gasSelection.title: Shielding gas selection
problems: Weld quality is unstable with the current gas mix.
Porosity, spatter, oxidation, or poor weld appearance occurs.
Gas consumption is high, but quality does not improve.
The gas is selected by habit, not by material and process.
causes: Gas mixture, flow, nozzle, or electrode stickout does not match the material and shielding conditions.
Drafts, joint access, welding position, or equipment settings affect shielding.
analysisItems: Checking material, MIG/MAG or TIG process, thickness, welding position, and weld requirements.
Reviewing the current gas mix, flow rate, nozzle, electrode stickout, and shielding conditions.
Comparing gas options by quality, speed, appearance, and cost.
Checking the effect of drafts, joint access, and equipment settings.
solutionSteps: Match weld requirements with possible gas mixtures and a flow range.
Verify the chosen option using real joint access and actual parameters.
expectedResults: A justified shielding gas choice or gas mix range.
More stable weld pool shielding and weld quality.
Reduced unnecessary gas consumption where possible.
A clearer link between gas, parameters, and result.

training.title: Personnel training
problems: New welders do not produce stable quality.
Errors repeat because process causes are not explained.
Production depends on a few experienced employees.
Technical requirements exist, but personnel apply them unevenly.
causes: People know separate techniques but not the link between settings, technique, and defects.
Training is not tied to real parts, requirements, and common shop-floor mistakes.
analysisItems: Assessing current welder skill level and typical mistakes.
Checking understanding of parameters, part preparation, torch technique, and weld inspection.
Defining training topics for the specific process and production tasks.
Connecting practical exercises with real defects and quality requirements.
solutionSteps: Build training around the specific process, material, and common defects.
Practice with clear control and repeatability criteria.
expectedResults: A more consistent skill level across employees.
Fewer recurring mistakes and defects.
Practical skills tied to real products and processes.
Understanding not only how to weld, but why defects appear.

wpsSupport.title: Project support / WPS implementation
problems: The process needs a stable launch, but parameters are not documented yet.
WPS or pWPS exists formally, but production does not apply it consistently.
Customer requirements, audits, or projects require traceability.
Documentation, real parameters, and quality are not connected well enough.
causes: Documentation does not reflect actual equipment, joint, and workplace constraints.
Parameters have not been checked under the conditions where production will make real parts.
analysisItems: Checking project requirements, material, joints, equipment, and available processes.
Reviewing existing WPS/pWPS, process sheets, and actual parameters.
Comparing documentation with what happens at the workplace.
Defining which parameters should be fixed, checked, or validated on samples.
solutionSteps: Align WPS/pWPS with actual parameters, control points, and welder actions.
Fix the parameters needed for launch, control, and traceability.
expectedResults: A clearer WPS implementation in real production.
Aligned parameters and actions for welders, supervisors, and technologists.
Fewer gaps between documentation and practice.
Readiness for internal control, customer requirements, or audits.

about.fallbackBio:
I am a Welding Engineer (IWE) with hands-on production experience and teaching background. My journey in welding began in 2011 after completing training in MMA and MAG processes at the 3rd Riga Vocational School.

Over the years as a welder, I gained experience in various production companies, from repair welding work to manufacturing rebar frameworks and metal structures. This provided me with a deep understanding of a welder's work in real conditions and the difference between theory and practice.

For nearly three years, I taught materials science, welding technology, and practical welding classes at a training center in Riga, focusing on skills directly applicable in the workplace.

Currently, I work as a Welding Engineer in an international company specializing in gas production and sales. In this role, I collaborate with managers, advise on the selection of shielding and combustible gases, conduct testing, participate in welding technology adjustments, and optimize process quality and stability.

I am the author of a book on MAG/MIG welding. I hold a Bachelor's and Master's degree in Engineering (Instrumentation) from Riga Technical University. I have completed additional training: a Welding Coordination course according to DVS-IIW 1170 — International Welding Engineer (IWE), International Welding Engineer (IWE).

calculators.engineeringNote: Use the calculated value as a technical starting point. Final settings should be checked against material, joint access, WPS requirements, equipment limits, and trial weld results.
calculators.validationCtaTitle: Only if the result needs review
calculators.validationCtaText: Request consultation if the calculated parameters are outside the expected range, conflict with WPS limits, or need production validation.

heat-input.lead: Estimates heat input (kJ/mm) from voltage, current and travel speed. For welding engineers and technicians comparing WPS values and thermal load.
heat-input.exampleCaption: Two different heat-input levels: higher Q usually means more energy per unit length in the weld.

gas-flow.lead: Estimates gas consumption over welding time and relates it to cylinder volume. Helpful when planning jobs and cylinder stock.
gas-flow.exampleCaption: Flow rate multiplied by time gives volume; compare with cylinder capacity for run time.

shielding-gas.lead: Suggests a reasonable shielding gas flow range from wire size, material and process. Use as a starting point before fine-tuning with tests.
shielding-gas.exampleCaption: Min–max band with a typical setpoint; adjust for nozzle, draft and joint access.

gas-cutting.lead: Oxygen cutting: indicative O₂ pressure and fuel flow from plate thickness (and optional cutting speed). Always verify with equipment manuals and trials.
gas-cutting.exampleCaption: Thicker plate generally needs higher oxygen pressure; values are indicative.

welding-cost.lead: Rough cost split between filler wire and shielding gas from prices, deposition rate and time. For estimators and workshop planning.
welding-cost.exampleCaption: Illustrative share of wire vs gas; your actual split depends on parameters and prices.

welding-parameters.lead: Starting-point current, voltage and travel speed from plate thickness, joint and wire diameter. Confirm on samples and your WPS.
welding-parameters.exampleCaption: Example parameter set (I, U, travel speed) for a typical MAG fillet — not a substitute for procedure qualification.

hints.voltage: Arc or load voltage used in the heat-input formula (check whether your WPS uses measured arc voltage).
hints.current: Welding current in amperes; must match the process and wire size you use.
hints.travelSpeed: Torch travel speed along the joint; must be greater than zero. Use consistent units (mm/min here).

hints.flowRate: Shielding gas flow at the torch (L/min), as set on the flowmeter or regulator.
hints.weldingTime: Total arc time in minutes for the calculation period (not necessarily clock time).
hints.cylinderVolume: Gas volume of the full cylinder in litres (often stated on the cylinder or data sheet).

hints.wireDiameter: Filler wire diameter; larger wires often allow a slightly wider flow window.
hints.material: Base material group (steel, stainless, aluminium) affects recommended shielding and flow.
hints.process: MIG/MAG or TIG — different torch and shielding behaviour.

hints.plateThickness: Thickness of the plate to cut; drives oxygen pressure and cutting setup.
hints.gasType: Fuel gas type (e.g. acetylene or propane) affects fuel flow recommendations.
hints.cuttingSpeed: Optional: actual cutting speed to refine estimates; leave empty if unknown.

hints.wirePrice: Purchase price per kilogram of filler wire.
hints.gasPrice: Price per full cylinder of shielding gas (same units as in your quote).
hints.cylinderVolume: Gas content of one cylinder in litres, for consumption and cost conversion.
hints.depositionRate: Mass of metal deposited per hour for your parameters (from datasheets or measurements).
hints.weldingTime: Arc hours for the job or batch being estimated.

hints.plateThickness: Main plate thickness in the joint; primary input for suggested heat.
hints.jointType: Butt, fillet, lap or corner — influences recommended parameters.
hints.wireDiameter: Filler wire diameter used in the process.
